transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Liam Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Head of ML, Vanguard Tech), Ethan Cole (Platform Eng), Ruth Delgado (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto gen): Vanguard evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted/Private. Primary drivers: isolation for regulated customers, predictable throughput for nightly batch and daytime interactive burst, and the ability to run on-prem for a subset of customers.

[00:00] Liam Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining. quick intros on our side, i'm liam park, account exec. Sofia's our solutions eng, she'll do the technical lift.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hi all, priya here — head of ml. We run inference for personalized recommendations and a new assistant product. We have some regulatory customers who require data not leave their VPC, so that's driving interest in private/dedicated options.
[00:31] Sofia Ramirez: Great, thanks priya. quick question — is the VPC requirement per-customer (tenant) or just for specific regulated flows?
[00:40] Priya Nair: It's a subset. about ~15% of our enterprise customers need full isolation and proof of data residency. The rest are fine with cloud-hosted as long as it's encrypted and auditable.
[00:55] Ethan Cole: And on traffic patterns: we have pretty spiky QPS. daytime baseline is 80–120 qps, then we have nightly jobs that push 4–6k qps for short bursts, like 20–30 minutes, for batch enrichment. That's what we're worried about for capacity and costs.
[01:15] Liam Park: Alright that's helpful. high level, Redwood supports three modes — Hosted API for quick ramp, Dedicated reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation, and Private for VPC/on-prem. For your use case sounds like a hybrid could fit — Dedicated for the regular traffic plus a plan for controlled burst capacity or fallback to Hosted for overflow.
[01:35] Ruth Delgado: Can you explain how Redwood's burst model works? We can't have long cold starts for dedicated nodes, and we need guarantees around p99 latency.
[01:45] Sofia Ramirez: sure. for dedicated, customers reserve a pool of GPU capacity. we support autoscaling within the pool and also burst policies — you can configure burst to use either unallocated cloud capacity or pre-assigned burst credit. important: bursts are subject to region availability and we've got rules for fallbacks to compatible model variants to preserve latency.
[02:05] Priya Nair: what about the cost? bursting to hosted sounds cheaper in some cases but then data leaves the private pool, which is an issue for those 15% customers.
[02:16] Liam Park: Exactly — that's the tradeoff. Many teams use a mixed routing policy: route regulated tenants to Dedicated/Private always, and others to Hosted during extreme bursts. If you need absolute on-prem isolation for some customers, we can support Private deployments with a customer-managed control plane — no egress.
[02:36] Ethan Cole: if we go Private for those 15%, can the same model versions be served across Dedicated and Private so we don't have divergence?
[02:45] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, the deployment abstraction lets you pin model versions and rollout policies. The same artifact can be deployed to hosted, dedicated, or private clusters; the runtime handles kernel selection and quantization variants. There can be small differences in latency depending on hardware and quantization, but functionally it's the same model.
[03:06] [background noise, slight crosstalk]
[03:20] Priya Nair: On latency, our target is p99 < 2s for interactive inference. Nightly batch jobs can be relaxed. Will dedicated get us there?
[03:30] Sofia Ramirez: With properly sized pools and kernel/sequence tuning we often hit sub-second p99 on Llama2-ish workloads at typical token lengths. The big knobs are batching, KV cache locality for chat-like workloads, and quantization. For deterministic p99 we recommend dedicated capacity pinned to a commit and a small headroom buffer (10–20%) to absorb spikes.
[03:57] Ruth Delgado: What about lifecycle — model rollouts, canarying? we need to be able to rollback quickly if a new model regresses.
[04:08] Liam Park: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You can set rollout percentages and have automatic fallback to a prior model or a smaller variant if latency or error rate increases.
[04:25] Ethan Cole: On the ops side, what SLA do you offer for Dedicated? We need uptime and latency guarantees for our SLAs to customers.
[04:33] Sofia Ramirez: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets on our reserved tiers. specifics depend on contract level — we can share typical SLA numbers in the doc pack.
[04:45] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk about burst sizing. Our nightly surge is 4–6k qps for ~25 minutes. Do you typically recommend over-provisioning or using burst credits?
[04:57] Sofia Ramirez: There's two common patterns: 1) reserve enough GPUs to handle baseline and moderate spikes and use burst credits for rare extremes; or 2) reserve more aggressive dedicated pools to keep everything internal. The first reduces cost but needs careful routing to ensure regulated tenants aren't routed off-prem. If those bursts are frequent (e.g., daily), reserved capacity is usually more predictable and can be cheaper than repeated burst consumption.
[05:25] Priya Nair: They're nightly and predictable, so maybe reserved makes sense. but cost is still a concern. can you provide some cost modeling?
[05:33] Liam Park: absolutely, we'll send a cost model. we'll ask for your workload traces so Sofia can model token distribution, sequence length, and concurrency to estimate GPU-hours and recommended reservation.
[05:44] Ruth Delgado: Security — we need SOC 2, SSO, audit logs, KMS. How mature is Redwood on that?
[05:52] Liam Park: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integrations (customer-managed KMS for private). We have SOC 2 reports and can share compliance artifacts. For on-prem Private, you can keep the control plane private and integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[06:10] Ethan Cole: For VPC peering, what networking requirements exist? Do we need BGP or specific route setups?
[06:18] Sofia Ramirez: For Private we typically use VPC peering or private link options. There's a network design doc we'll share — it covers IP ranges, peering, firewall rules, and NAT options for restricted environments.
[06:32] [00:06:32 — pause while sharing doc link in chat]
[06:40] Priya Nair: Can you describe the benchmark process? we'd like to run a two-hour benchmark with our payloads.
[06:45] Sofia Ramirez: Sure. Typical benchmark steps: 1) customer provides representative traces and sample prompts; 2) we produce a job that replays traffic at desired QPS and distribution; 3) run on both Dedicated candidate config and Hosted fallback; 4) collect token-level latency, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates, and cost per token. We can also test quantization/compile variants.
[07:12] Ruth Delgado: How do you handle cold-start effects for model weights and KV cache? Our chat workloads are sensitive to first-token latency spikes.
[07:22] Sofia Ramirez: Good point. We have pre-warming options, and we maintain warm pools that keep model artifacts resident. For chat, KV cache locality is important — continuous batching and small headroom help avoid those p99 spikes. Cold starts typically affect the very first request after scale-up; we can configure keep-alive to mitigate.
[07:45] Ethan Cole: If we need on-prem, what's the installation footprint? GPU requirements, kube versions?
[07:53] Sofia Ramirez: For on-prem/private deployments we support common distributions Kubernetes 1.25+ typically, NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA 12+ recommended. We'll share an architecture guide with exact node sizing guidance.
[08:07] Priya Nair: Do you provide managed services for Private? We may not have a big infra team.
[08:14] Liam Park: Yes, enterprise plans often include a managed offering where Redwood supports control plane ops and patching. Alternatively, teams can self-manage with our install bundle and we provide remote support.
[08:28] [08:28 — brief crosstalk]
[08:37] Priya Nair: Quick question — what about multitenancy? we want per-tenant isolation for the regulated set but also consolidated models for easier updates.
[08:45] Sofia Ramirez: You can do logical isolation (namespace, RBAC, per-tenant routing) and physical isolation (separate Dedicated pools or Private clusters). Many teams use logical isolation for non-regulated tenants and physical isolation for regulated ones.
[09:00] Priya Nair: Any caveats with model variants and quantization across different hardware? we want consistent outputs for A/B testing.
[09:10] Sofia Ramirez: Quantization and different kernel implementations can introduce tiny numeric differences, but we try to match float32 behavior with debug builds for eval. For strict A/B you can pin the same runtime config or keep a single deployment and route.
[09:30] Ethan Cole: On auditing, do you capture token-level logs? That could be sensitive.
[09:36] Liam Park: We capture metadata and optionally token-level logs depending on config and retention. For regulated data we recommend redacting or using on-prem Private where logs can be kept entirely in customer control.
[09:55] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk timeframe — we're aiming to pilot in Q1. what's a realistic timeline to go from contract to pilot?
[10:05] Liam Park: For Dedicated hosted pilot with reserved pools typically 4–6 weeks — that includes sizing, contract, and a benchmark run. For Private/on-prem it's 6–12 weeks depending on approvals and infra readiness.
[10:18] Ruth Delgado: Do you support heterogeneous GPU fleets? e.g., mix of H100 and A100? We have some older infra.
[10:27] Sofia Ramirez: We support heterogeneous fleets but runtime kernel selection matters — we can route workloads to compatible instances for latency-critical paths. Mixing GPUs is fine but you should expect different perf characteristics.
[10:40] Priya Nair: What's the typical headroom you recommend for p99 guarantees?
[10:45] Sofia Ramirez: 10–25% buffer depending on burst predictability. For highly bursty daily jobs, we recommend a higher buffer or scheduling batch windows to smooth load.
[10:55] Ethan Cole: If we wanted autoscaling on Dedicated, how fast can it scale? seconds? minutes?
[11:02] Sofia Ramirez: Scaling is in the order of minutes for new GPUs to be attached in cloud environments; if you need sub-minute response you should keep warm capacity or use pre-warmed burst pools.
[11:16] [11:16 — short pause while Liam types a note]
[11:25] Priya Nair: Let's get into some concrete numbers — i'll share a 7-day trace with token lengths and concurrency tomorrow. can you take a swing at recommended reserved GPUs?
[11:35] Liam Park: Absolutely. once we have those traces Sofia will run a cost/perf model and propose a recommendation: baseline reserved pool + suggested burst sizing.
[11:44] Ruth Delgado: Any legal hurdles around data residency if we use Hosted for non-regulated tenants?
[11:50] Liam Park: We support region pinning and data residency controls; legal team can review the DPA and addendum for regulated accounts.
[12:00] Priya Nair: ok great. one last question — how do you handle regressions detection? we need alerts when model quality drops after rollout.
[12:08] Sofia Ramirez: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tie-ins to prompt sets and evals. You can set regression alerts on specific prompt sets and automatically halt rollouts.
[12:20] Ethan Cole: I'm curious about caching — can we do prefix caching across tenants to reduce load?
[12:27] Sofia Ramirez: yes, prefix and KV caching are supported. be careful with privacy boundaries — don't share across regulated tenants unless allowed.
[12:36] [12:36 — soft laughter]
[12:40] Liam Park: ok to recap — action items: we'll send pricing/ cost model, Sofia will draft a benchmark plan and we need the traces from Priya. we'll also share SOC2 and the network architecture doc. Pilot timeline targeted Q1.
[12:56] Priya Nair: That sounds good. we'll get traces and schedule the benchmark in the next week. thanks for the clear options.
[13:06] Ruth Delgado: thanks liam and sofia. this was productive.
[13:12] Liam Park: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the doc bundle and scheduling links.

End of transcript.
